title: Detection of Query Public AI Services
shortTitle: Detection of Query Public AI Services
summary: This detection strategy covers outbound access from the estate to public generative artificial intelligence (AI) services, whether that access is a careless upload of protected data or an adversary using hosted models for tooling such as text rewriting, translation or code generation. It covers technique T1682 and matters because the request leaves the organisation's control while the response can be used directly in an intrusion workflow, and because content sent to a public service is a data loss event in itself. The telemetry that makes it possible is web proxy and next generation firewall logs with server name indication and application category, Domain Name System (DNS) query logs, TLS client fingerprints, and endpoint process creation showing which program made the connection. In practice the strategy fails because most traffic is encrypted, approved assistants are widespread, and the same endpoints are used for legitimate work, so category based alerts alone generate heavy noise. Correlating destination category with the requesting account, the uploading process and data volume is what makes the alert useful.

beginner.definition: Public artificial intelligence (AI) services are websites that answer questions and create content. This detection watches for computers in your network that send data to them. It catches both risky data sharing and attacker use.
beginner.whyItMatters: When you send text to a public service, you lose control of it. A worker may paste customer data by mistake. An attacker may use the same service to clean up text or write code. Both cases matter, and both look like ordinary web traffic. So you must look at who and what.
howItWorks: You collect web proxy and firewall logs. These record the destination and the amount of data sent.
You collect Domain Name System (DNS) queries, which show the service name being looked up.
You classify the destination into a category, such as generative artificial intelligence.
You identify the process and the user account behind the connection.
You measure upload volume. A few kilobytes is a question. Many megabytes is a document.
You alert when a blocked category, an unusual program or a large upload appears together.
beginner.example: Think of a company post box. Sending a letter is normal and fine. But if someone posts a thick folder of customer files every afternoon, the post room should ask what is inside. The address is not the problem. The amount, the sender and the timing are what draw attention. Querying a public AI service works exactly like that folder.
takeaways: The same destination can be harmless for one team and a policy breach for another.
Upload volume and the requesting program are the most useful fields.
You cannot read encrypted content, so you detect the behaviour around it instead.

objectives: Explain why traffic to public artificial intelligence (AI) services is relevant to both data protection and intrusion detection
Read web proxy, firewall and Domain Name System (DNS) logs to identify which hosts reach AI service endpoints
Use TLS client fingerprints and process creation records to determine which program initiated the session
Set upload volume thresholds that separate a single question from a bulk document submission
Describe the limits of detection when traffic is encrypted and inspection is not performed
Propose an approved alternative service and a policy path so that blocking does not push users to personal devices
dataSources: Web proxy or secure web gateway logs with destination category, server name indication (SNI), bytes uploaded and authenticated user
Next generation firewall application control records identifying the recognised application and the client process where available
Domain Name System (DNS) query logs listing lookups for public generative artificial intelligence service hostnames per internal host
Transport Layer Security client hello metadata expressed as a JA3 or JA4 fingerprint, used to identify the client library making the request
Windows Security event 4688 process creation or Linux audit execution records showing the browser, command line tool or script that opened the session
logic: The pattern is repeated, deliberate outbound contact with public generative artificial intelligence endpoints from hosts whose role does not explain it, especially when upload volume is high or the client is a script rather than a browser. You correlate the destination category or server name indication from proxy and firewall logs with DNS lookups for the same host, the account and device behind the session, and the process recorded at connection time. The malicious or high risk case is a non browser client such as a command line tool posting large bodies of text, repeated calls at machine like intervals, or contact from a server or service account that has no business reaching an external model. The benign case is an employee using a browser to ask a short question, or an approved enterprise assistant reached through an allowlisted endpoint. Session volume per user per day is the simplest field that separates the two.
pseudoQuery:
# title: High Volume Upload to Public Generative AI Service
# logsource:
#   product: network
#   service: proxy
# detection:
#   selection:
#     destination_category: 'generative-ai'
#     bytes_out: > 5000000
#   filter_approved:
#     destination_domain:
#       - 'assistant.corp.example'
#       - 'approved-ai-partner.example'
#   condition: selection and not filter_approved
# level: medium
falsePositives: Developers using an approved but locally installed coding assistant that reaches a public model endpoint
Marketing staff generating image or copy variants in a browser as part of a documented campaign workflow
Accessibility features such as live captioning or translation that stream audio or text to an external service
Software update and telemetry channels of products that embed a third party model for autocomplete features
Security research or threat intelligence teams querying public models to summarise reports during an investigation
tuningNotes: Start by allowlisting approved enterprise assistant endpoints and by creating a per user daily volume baseline for each business unit, then alert on deviations from that baseline rather than on a fixed byte count. Scope the rule to hosts that hold regulated data, such as finance, human resources and engineering repositories, and keep a lower severity rule for the rest of the estate. Filter browser sessions from short question and answer use, but keep alerting on non browser clients and service accounts. Excluding approved destinations means you will miss sensitive data pasted into an approved tool, so add data loss prevention coverage on the approved path as a compensating control.
